body:
Social reform was not confined to princely governments

During the 19th century, important reform initiatives also emerged in British-administered towns of Gujarat. Teachers, writers, journalists and public associations challenged social customs and encouraged education and debate.

These activities should be studied alongside the reforms of princely Baroda because they addressed related problems through different methods. State-directed reform relied on governmental institutions and regulations, while voluntary social reform relied largely on meetings, publications, schools, associations and public opinion.

Manav Dharma Sabha: Surat, 1844

The Manav Dharma Sabha was established in Surat in 1844. Durgaram Manchharam Mehta was a leading founder, along with Dadoba Pandurang and other associates.

The Sabha questioned religious superstition and caste distinctions and encouraged discussion of social and moral reform. Its ideas included the view that people should be judged by their conduct rather than by inherited caste position. It was associated with the wider movement to improve the position of women and challenge restrictive social practices.

The importance of the Sabha lies in the emergence of organised social criticism among educated Indians in Gujarat. It was a reform association in Surat, not a department established by the Gaekwad ruler of Baroda.

Gujarat Vernacular Society: Ahmedabad, 1848

The Gujarat Vernacular Society was established in Ahmedabad in 1848 through the initiative of Alexander Kinloch Forbes, a British official with a strong interest in Gujarati language and literature.

The Society encouraged Gujarati education and literary activity by promoting books, manuscripts, publications and the work of writers. Its purpose was to make useful knowledge available through the regional language rather than restricting intellectual activity to English.

Dalpatram, the Gujarati poet and writer, was closely associated with Forbes and later played an important role in the Society. He also edited Buddhiprakash, a periodical associated with Gujarati learning and public discussion.

The Society opened a public library in 1849. This was an important early institution for access to books in Ahmedabad.

The Gujarat Vernacular Society's public library in 1849 and Baroda State's organised public library movement in 1910 were different developments. One was associated with a voluntary literary society in Ahmedabad; the other developed into a coordinated state library service in princely Baroda.

Other prominent Gujarati reformers

Several writers and public figures contributed to the broader movement for social and educational change:

  • Narmadashankar Lalshankar Dave, commonly called Narmad: Advocated social reform and challenged restrictions associated with caste and widow remarriage.
  • Karsandas Mulji: Used Gujarati journalism to criticise social and religious abuses. He established the reformist newspaper Satya Prakash in 1855.
  • Mahipatram Rupram Nilkanth: Worked in education and supported reform concerning women's education and social practices.
  • Dalpatram: Contributed to Gujarati literature and the development of public education through his association with the Gujarat Vernacular Society.

These reformers were not interchangeable. Some worked primarily through literature or journalism, while others were associated with educational institutions and organised associations. Their contributions complemented, but were distinct from, governmental reforms in princely states.

Public institutions in British and princely Gujarat

British-administered towns also developed municipal institutions. For example, Surat's municipality was founded in 1852. Such bodies dealt with local civic matters within the colonial administrative framework.

By contrast, Baroda's educational, library and public-works institutions formed part of a princely administration. These distinctions matter because the same broad objective, such as improving education or public welfare, could be pursued by different types of institutions.

Putting the major events in order

A useful way to remember this period is to distinguish early public associations from the later institutional reforms of Sayajirao's reign. The Manav Dharma Sabha and Gujarat Vernacular Society emerged before Sayajirao became ruler. Baroda's later achievements included higher and technical education, compulsory schooling, banking and an organised library network.

The central distinction

Baroda's significance lies in the use of princely governmental authority to establish or expand public institutions. Surat and Ahmedabad demonstrate the importance of writers, associations and civic institutions in British-administered Gujarat. Both contributed to change, but their political authority and methods of reform differed.

Reform outcomes also require careful interpretation. The establishment of a school, law, library or association created an opportunity or institution; it did not by itself guarantee that poverty, illiteracy, caste exclusion or inequality had disappeared.

Prelims focus

  • 1844, Surat: Manav Dharma Sabha, associated with Durgaram Mehta and Dadoba Pandurang.
  • 1848, Ahmedabad: Gujarat Vernacular Society, founded through the initiative of A. K. Forbes.
  • Dalpatram was associated with the Gujarat Vernacular Society and Buddhiprakash.
  • 1849: The Gujarat Vernacular Society opened a public library in Ahmedabad.
  • 1910: Baroda's organised public library movement developed under Sayajirao III.
  • Trap: An early public library in Ahmedabad is not the same institution as the later state-wide library system of princely Baroda.

title: Gujarat's Nineteenth-Century Reform Associations and the Main Chronological Distinctions
